opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because the priorities really do shift quite a bit along that journey.

In the early phase, when an enterprise is evaluating an AI application, the overwhelming focus is on quality. Can this thing actually do the task? Is the accuracy good enough? Does it handle the edge cases that matter for our business? At that stage, people are usually willing to use the biggest, most capable model available, they don't worry too much about cost, and latency is often secondary. You're trying to answer a basic question: is there real value here?

Once you've convinced yourself that the answer is yes, and you start thinking about deploying at scale, the picture changes. Cost becomes a first-class concern very quickly. Something that costs a few cents per request is fine when you're running a pilot with a hundred users, but when you're serving millions of requests a day, that adds up to real money. So people start asking: can we use a smaller model? Can we fine-tune or distill something that's cheaper but still good enough on our specific task? Can we route easy queries to cheap models and only send the hard ones to the expensive ones?

Latency and reliability also become much more important. In production, you have SLAs, you have users who expect a responsive experience, and you need the system to stay up and behave predictably. Then there's a whole set of concerns around security, privacy, and governance: where is the data going, who has access to it, can we audit what the model did, are we compliant with regulations in the industries and regions we operate in. For many enterprises, that pushes them toward having more control, sometimes running models in their own environment rather than only calling external APIs.

And finally, observability and continuous improvement. In evaluation you test against a fixed benchmark, but in production the data drifts, users do unexpected things, and you need infrastructure to monitor quality, catch regressions, and feed that back into improving the system.

So I'd summarize it this way: at the beginning it's "can it work?", and at scale it becomes "can it work reliably, affordably, securely, and keep getting better?" That's a big part of why the infrastructure and systems side of AI matters so much. The models get the headlines, but making them practical at scale is fundamentally a systems problem.

r001.rationale: The response says early evaluation focuses overwhelmingly on quality and real value, with little concern for cost; cost becomes a first-class concern at scale.

r002.rationale: As deployment scales, the response says security, privacy, and governance concerns can push enterprises toward more control, including running models in their own environment.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly identifies security as a concern that becomes important in production at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think there's a pretty clear shift, and it maps onto what we've seen at Databricks and Anyscale, and now with what we're doing around evaluation and routing.

When an enterprise starts out, the only thing that matters is: does it work? They take a frontier model, they build a prototype, maybe a RAG pipeline or an agent, and the question is purely about quality. Can it answer the question, can it do the task. Cost doesn't matter, latency doesn't matter, because you're running ten queries a day in a demo. And honestly, at that stage they usually go with the biggest, most capable model they can get access to, because that gives them the best chance of showing it works at all.

Then something interesting happens when it moves into production. Three things come in that were basically invisible before. The first is cost. If you go from ten queries to ten million queries, suddenly the per-token price of the frontier model is a line item that the CFO sees. The second is latency, because now there's a real user or a real workflow waiting on the response, and a five-second answer that was fine in a demo is not fine in a customer-facing product. And the third, which I think is underrated, is reliability and control. In a demo, if the model does something weird one time in twenty, you shrug. In production, one in twenty is a disaster. And on top of that you have questions around data privacy, where the data goes, who sees it, can you run it inside your own environment.

So what you see is the priority stack flips. It starts as quality, quality, quality. And it ends up as: quality at a given cost, with a given latency, under a given set of constraints. And that's a much harder optimization problem, because you now have multiple dimensions and you have to make trade-offs.

The practical consequence is that nobody at scale uses a single model for everything. You end up with a portfolio. Maybe a frontier model for the hard, high-value queries, and smaller open models, often fine-tuned on your own data, for the bulk of the traffic. And then the question becomes, how do you decide which query goes where? That's the routing problem, and I think it's going to be one of the core pieces of infrastructure for every serious deployment.

The other thing that changes is evaluation. Early on, evaluation is a human looking at outputs and saying, yeah, that looks good. At scale, that doesn't work. You need systematic, continuous evaluation, because the model changes, your data changes, user behavior changes, and you need to know when quality drifts. I'd actually argue that most enterprises underinvest in this, and it's the thing that bites them later.

So to summarize, it goes from "can it work" to "can it work reliably, at a cost and latency I can afford, with the control I need." And the companies that make that transition well are the ones that treat it as a systems problem, not just a model problem.

r001.rationale: It says early evaluation focuses on whether the application works and that cost does not matter, but it does not state that establishing business value is the priority.

r002.rationale: It describes control as a production concern, including data location and running the application in the enterprise’s own environment, and says scaled deployments must meet those constraints.

r003.rationale: It mentions data privacy as a concern at scale, but does not state that security becomes a greater priority.

astra-6.text:
I think the priorities shift from capability to reliability and economics. In the evaluation phase, the question is, can this model solve my problem? You try a few examples, compare the quality, and see whether there is value.

When you move to production, quality is still critical, but now you care about latency, cost, security, and how the application interacts with your existing data and systems. Can you meet those requirements consistently, across the actual requests your users send?

At scale, even a small cost per request can become significant. So you start asking whether you need the most capable model for every request, or whether a smaller model can handle some of the work. You also need monitoring and evaluation as you change the system. The focus expands from the model itself to operating the entire application reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says initial evaluation checks whether the application provides value, while it raises cost as a production and scale concern.

r002.rationale: It discusses monitoring, evaluation, and operating the application reliably, but does not clearly state that enterprises place greater emphasis on control over deployment as they scale a use case with established business value.

r003.rationale: The response names security among the requirements that matter in production, after describing initial evaluation as focused on capability and value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the priorities shift from, “Can this model do the task?” to, “Can we operate this application reliably and economically?” In the initial evaluation, people focus on quality. They try different models, build a prototype, and see whether it solves a useful problem.

When you move to production, quality is still critical, but now you have latency requirements, cost constraints, security, and integration with your existing data and systems. And quality becomes something you have to measure continuously, because the inputs can change and the models can change.

At scale, these things are connected. A larger model might give you better results, but if it is too slow or too expensive for the workload, it may not be the right choice for every request. So the focus moves from choosing a model to building and operating the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response says initial evaluation focuses on quality and whether the prototype solves a useful problem, but it does not state that business value takes priority over cost.

r002.rationale: It describes operating the whole system at scale, but does not state that enterprises place greater emphasis on control over deployment.

r003.rationale: It contrasts initial evaluation, where people focus on quality, with production, where security becomes one of the added priorities.
